computer-science.title: Computer science: search and data structures
computer-science.text:
Linear search checks elements in sequence and works on an unsorted array. In the worst case, it examines all n elements, giving O(n) time.

Binary search requires a sorted array with random access. Each comparison discards about half the remaining search range. Its worst-case time is O(log n).

A stack follows last-in, first-out order. A queue follows first-in, first-out order. A stack removes the most recently added item; a queue removes the earliest added item.

Breadth-first search explores a graph in layers using a queue. Depth-first search follows a path deeply before backtracking, using a stack or recursion. On an unweighted graph, breadth-first search can find a path with the fewest edges.

psychology.title: Psychology: learning and research methods
psychology.text:
Classical conditioning involves learning an association between stimuli. An initially neutral stimulus can come to elicit a learned response after pairing with a stimulus that already elicits a response.

Operant conditioning concerns how consequences influence behavior. Reinforcement increases the likelihood of a behavior; punishment decreases it. Positive means adding a stimulus, while negative means removing a stimulus. Negative reinforcement therefore removes a stimulus to increase behavior; it is not punishment.

Observational learning involves learning by watching another person's behavior and its consequences. Direct personal reinforcement is not required for every instance of observational learning.

A correlation describes an association between measured variables and alone does not establish causation. In a controlled experiment, researchers manipulate an independent variable and measure a dependent variable. Random assignment helps balance potential confounding variables between experimental groups.

physics.title: Physics: force and mechanical energy
physics.text:
Newton's second law relates net force, mass, and acceleration: F = m*a. For motion along one axis, the sign of acceleration follows the sign of net force when mass is positive. Force is measured in newtons, mass in kilograms, and acceleration in metres per second squared.

Translational kinetic energy is K = (1/2)*m*v^2, measured in joules. With fixed mass, doubling speed multiplies kinetic energy by four. Speed is nonnegative.

Near Earth's surface, the change in gravitational potential energy relative to a chosen height reference is U = m*g*h. Use g = 9.8 metres per second squared. State the height reference and assume g is constant. Potential energy is measured in joules.

For a constant force parallel to displacement, work is W = F*d. Work is measured in joules. Here F is the component of force along the displacement, in newtons, and d is displacement in metres. These formulas support numerical exercises with specified masses, forces, speeds, heights, and distances.
